questions.question: Describe Maqoma's background and his expulsion from the Kat River valley.
questions.expected_answer: Born 1798, eldest son of Ngqika (Rharhabe Xhosa) by his first wife; heir was Sandile (son of the great wife), so Maqoma was senior son of the right-hand house and acted as regent after Ngqika died (1829); skilled warrior and orator with contacts with colonists and missionaries. Settled in the Kat River valley in the Ceded Territory in the 1820s; expelled in 1829 (accused of raiding the Thembu) and again in 1833 - homes burnt, land given to the Khoikhoi Kat River Settlement as a buffer; he felt betrayed.

questions.question: Explain Maqoma's role in the wars of 1834-1835 and 1850-1853.
questions.expected_answer: 1834-35: after land losses, reprisals and the shooting of a chief, Maqoma and Tyhali led Xhosa forces into the colony, taking cattle; retreated to the Amathole to fight a guerrilla war against D'Urban and Harry Smith; Hintsa killed; Queen Adelaide Province returned (1836). 1850-53 (Mlanjeni's War): after the annexation of British Kaffraria, Smith's humiliation of chiefs and the deposing of Sandile, Maqoma led skilful guerrilla resistance from the Amathole and Waterkloof forests, ambushing British columns for months, with Kat River Khoikhoi joining; ended by British scorched-earth tactics; more land lost.

questions.question: Why is Maqoma remembered as a hero of resistance?
questions.expected_answer: He defended his people's right to their land through diplomacy and then armed struggle; he was one of the greatest Xhosa military leaders, respected even by British officers, with effective guerrilla tactics; an eloquent speaker; he was imprisoned on Robben Island (1857-1869, again from 1871) and died there in 1873 - linking him to later resistance leaders imprisoned there such as Mandela; his remains were reburied at Ntaba kaNdoda in 1978.
